arXiv:2511.21033v1 [cs.AI] 26 Nov 2025

Towards Trustworthy Legal AI through LLM Agents and Formal Reasoning

Linze Chen Yufan Cai    Zhe Hou    Jinsong Dong
Abstract

The rationality of law manifests in two forms: substantive rationality, which concerns the fairness or moral desirability of outcomes, and formal rationality, which requires that legal decisions to follow explicitly stated, general, and logically coherent rules. Existing LLM‐based systems excel at surface‐level text analysis but lack the guarantees required for principled jurisprudence. We introduce L4M, a novel framework that combines adversarial LLM agents with SMT-solver–backed proofs to unite the interpretive flexibility of natural language with the rigor of symbolic verification. The pipeline consists of three phases: (1) Statute Formalization, where domain-specific prompts convert legal provisions into logical formulae; (2) Dual Fact–&–Statute Extraction, in which prosecutor‐ and defense‐aligned LLMs independently map case narratives to fact tuples and statutes, ensuring role isolation; (3) Solver‐Centric Adjudication, where an autoformalizer compiles both parties’ arguments into logic constraints, and unsat cores trigger iterative self‐critique until a satisfiable formula is achieved, which is verbalized by a Judge‐LLM into a transparent verdict and optimized sentence. Experimental results on the public benchmarks show that our system surpasses advanced LLMs including GPT‐o4-mini, DeepSeek-V3, and Claude 4 and the state-of-the-art baselines in Legal AI, while providing rigorous and explainable symbolic justifications.

1National University of Singapore

2Griffith University

1 Introduction

Legal decision‐making demands not only linguistic comprehension of statutory text but also formal rationality—the rigorous application of general, logically coherent rules (Weber 1968; Raz 1979). In modern rule‐of‐law systems, courts are constrained not to choose the result that feels morally best, but to justify outcomes by demonstrably fitting them under the governing rules and precedents.

Limitations of current legal NLP. Although recent Large Language Models (LLMs) can summarize opinions, draft pleadings (Hendrycks et al. 2021) and even pass bar‐exam questions (Katz et al. 2024), purely neural approaches still hallucinate authorities (Hou et al. 2024), blur doctrinal distinctions (Savelka 2023), and yield outputs that cannot be machine‐verified for consistency. Legal‐domain LLMs such as ChatLaw (Cui et al. 2023), LawLLM (Shu et al. 2024), and Lexi (Ho et al. 2025) mitigate factual errors via retrieval‐augmented generation, yet they stop short of symbolically proving that a conclusion follows from enacted statutes.

Towards neural–symbolic jurisprudence. To deliver trustworthy legal AI, we move beyond black‐box text generation and embed LLMs inside a logic–based control loop, resulting in our Legal Logic LLM (L4M) approach. We design a typed schema for statutory rules (§3) that captures actors, actions, conditions, and deontic status, then compile these into executable Z3 code. LLMs (i) extract candidate rules from raw provisions and (ii) map case narratives to weighted fact tuples, while an SMT solver verifies soundness, detects conflicts, and produces a proof object that a “Judge‐LLM” translates into plain‐language justifications. Early hybrid prototypes for tax compliance (Nay et al. 2023), and criminal sentencing (Li et al. 2023b) foreshadow the promise of this direction; our work extends it with a multi‐agent, adversarial pipeline that mirrors actual litigation dynamics.

To illustrate the performance of our approach, we conduct comprehensive evaluation on the public benchmark (Li et al. 2023a). Our system surpasses strong GPT‐o4‐mini, DeepSeek‐R1, and Claude‐4 baselines, improving statute‐selection and verdict sentence while emitting solver‐checked proofs that enable step‐by‐step auditability.

Contributions
  • •

    A interpretable formulation that supports informal and formal reasoning.

  • •

    An automated neural-symbolic workflow that extracts, formalizes, and verifies statutory reasoning via LLM agents and SMT solvers.

  • •

    Extensive experiments showing enhanced robustness, accuracy, and explainability over state‐of‐the‐art legal LLM baselines.

2 Motivating Example

In this section, we introduce a motivating example in real-world legal cases to show how our method works.

Case synopsis.

… (Gong Qiang concerns a repeat narcotics offender) Defendant Gong Qiang received a WeChat message from Luo, requesting the purchase of 1,000 yuan worth of drugs. After receiving the 1,000 yuan transfer from Luo via WeChat, Gong Qiang delivered 2 grams of methamphetamine and six magu tablets to Luo at approximately 5:00 PM that day …

Prosecutor Agent (accusatory stance) extracts:

  • •

    Actors: Defendant Gong Qiang (prior drug convictions), buyer Luo; public prosecution by Donghu District People’s Procuratorate.

  • •

    Acts: Sold 2 g methamphetamine + 6 “magu” tablets for 1 000 RMB.

  • •

    Evidence: WeChat payment record, seized drugs, positive urine tests, confession.

  • •

    Aggravators: Repeat drug offender within five-year window; multiple prior administrative penalties.

  • •

    Statutory Law: [64, 65]; [347, 356].

Defense Attorney Agent (exculpatory stance) extracts:

  • •

    Actors: Defendant Gong Qiang, buyer Luo; defense counsel appointed.

  • •

    Acts: Acknowledge sale but stress “very small quantity” and no wider circulation.

  • •

    Evidence: WeChat record, drug test, confession.

  • •

    Mitigators: Full confession, signed plea agreement, voluntary compensation and buyer’s understanding; prior sentence already served, limited social harm.

  • •

    Statutory Law: [64, 67]; [347, 356].

Structured Fact Extraction and Auto-formalizing

Then, LLMs converts the above natural language into structured representations and statute-specific entities with our defined formal schema. Table 1 provides two examples of statute-specific KB used in this module. We decompose the original fact set—which may involve multiple actions and legal aspects—into multiple slices, each dedicated to a specific statute. This stage operates in two steps:

(i) Formal schema based auto-formalizing

The prompt integrate the states from both prosecutor and attorney with a defined legal knowledge schema for general and specific provisions. The extracted facts were:

  • •

    General provisions: {illegal proceeds: True, prior sentence: True, reoffense_in_5_years: True, truthful_confession: True, recidivist_status: True}

  • •

    Specific provisions: {subject: [person], action: [traffic_narcotics], object: [narcotics], intent: [intentional]}

(ii) Intersection and slicing with statutes.

The system computes the intersection between extracted facts and defined statute schema, filtering irrelevant content and creating independent statute-fact slices. For example:

  • •

    Article 65: matched field { prior_sentence: True, reoffense_in_5_years: True }

  • •

    Article 67: matched field { truthful_confession: True }

  • •

    Article 347: matched fields {subject: person, action: traffic_narcotics, object: narcotics, intent: intentional}

Logic Verification with Formal Reasoner

Each statute is represented by a logical rule derived from Chinese Criminal Law, consisting of necessary conditions that must be satisfied for applicability. The Z3 solver evaluates these logical constraints against the extracted facts. Table 2 summarizes the pseudo-code and an example execution for Article 347. For the Gong Qiang case, the judge processed the candidate statutes as follows:

  • •

    Article 65 (Recidivism): Facts { reoffense_within_5_years=True } →\rightarrow retained.

  • •

    Article 67 (Mitigating Circumstance): Facts { truthful_confession=True } →\rightarrow retained.

  • •

    Article 347 (Drug Trafficking): Facts {subject=person, action=traffic narcotics, object=narcotics, intent=intentional} →\rightarrow retained.

The judge LLM outputs a structured fact representation specific to each statute, and a final sentence of 2 years and 10K yuan penalty. The ground truth is 1 year 2 months with 11K yuan penalty.

3 Approach

Our framework couples the open‐text understanding abilities of LLMs with the proof obligations enforced by an smt solver (Z3) in order to deliver auditable legal conclusions. Below we detail the two stages.

Stage 1: Legal Rule Formalization

Level 0—Formal Meta-schema.

We start from a universal first-order template that captures the quadruple Actor–Action–Condition–Norm, with penalty attached to the conclusion:

∀a:𝖠𝖼𝗍𝗈𝗋,α:𝖠𝖼𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇,κ:𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽𝗂𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇,n:𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆,p:𝖯𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗅𝗍𝗒.\displaystyle\forall a{:}{\sf Actor},\,\alpha{:}{\sf Action},\,\kappa{:}{\sf Condition},\,n{:}{\sf Norm},\,p{:}{\sf Penalty}.
𝗌𝖼𝗈𝗉𝖾⁡(n,a,α,κ)→𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗅𝗂𝖾𝗌⁡(n,a,α,κ,p).\displaystyle{\sf scope}(n,a,\alpha,\kappa)\;\rightarrow\;{\sf applies}(n,a,\alpha,\kappa,p). (1)

The sort 𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆{\sf Norm} is an element of prohibited, obligated, permitted, while 𝗌𝖼𝗈𝗉𝖾{\sf scope} will be progressively refined in the subsequent layers. The schema is globally consistent across all statutes, and every constraint field in downstream verification has a corresponding default extraction output.

Level 1—Article instantiation.

For a concrete statute article Arti\text{Art}_{i} we introduce an article guard 𝖺𝗋𝗍​_​𝗂{\sf art\_i} that fixes the overall applicability domain (jurisdiction, offense category, subject status, etc.). The formalized article is connected with the meta-schema by

𝗌𝖼𝗈𝗉𝖾⁡(⟨𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗁𝗂𝖻𝗂𝗍𝖾𝖽,Arti⟩,a,α,κ):≡𝖺𝗋𝗍​_​𝗂​(a,α,κ).{\sf scope}\!\bigl(\langle{\sf prohibited},\text{Art}_{i}\rangle,a,\alpha,\kappa\bigr)\;:\equiv\;{\sf art\_i}(a,\alpha,\kappa).

For example,

𝖺𝗋𝗍_𝗑(a,α,κ):≡\displaystyle{\sf art\_x}(a,\alpha,\kappa)\;:\equiv\;
𝖽𝗋𝗎𝗀(α)∧𝗁𝗈𝗅𝖽𝗌(κ.drug_type∈{meth,heroin})∧\displaystyle~~~~~{\sf drug}(\alpha)\;\land{\sf holds}\!\bigl(\kappa.\texttt{drug\_type}\!\in\!\{\textit{meth},\textit{heroin}\}\bigr)\;\land
𝗁𝖺𝗌​_​𝖼𝖺𝗉𝖺𝖼𝗂𝗍𝗒​(a,criminal_liability).\displaystyle~~~~~{\sf has\_capacity}\bigl(a,\textit{criminal\_liability}\bigr). (2)
Level 2—Clause instantiation.

Each article typically contains several clauses that refine quantitative thresholds or aggravating circumstances. Let Arti.cj\text{Art}_{i}.c_{j} denote clause jj of article ii. For each article, we define a clause guard 𝖼𝗅𝗂,𝗃{\sf cl_{i,j}} together with a statutory penalty range pi,jp_{i,j}. For example,

𝖼𝗅𝗂,𝟣​(κ):≡q1≤κ.qty<q2,pi,1=𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗀𝖾⁡(3,7)​ yrs;\displaystyle{\sf cl_{i,1}}(\kappa):\equiv q_{1}\leq\kappa.\text{qty}<q_{2},p_{i,1}={\sf range}(3,7)\text{~yrs}; (3)
𝖼𝗅𝗂,𝟤​(κ):≡q2≤κ.qty<q3,pi,2=𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗀𝖾⁡(7,15)​ yrs;\displaystyle{\sf cl_{i,2}}(\kappa):\equiv q_{2}\leq\kappa.\text{qty}<q_{3},p_{i,2}={\sf range}(7,15)\text{~yrs}; (4)
𝖼𝗅𝗂,𝟥​(κ):≡κ.qty≥q3,pi,3=𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗀𝖾⁡(15,∞)​ yrs.\displaystyle{\sf cl_{i,3}}(\kappa):\equiv\kappa.\text{qty}\geq q_{3},p_{i,3}={\sf range}(15,\infty)\text{~yrs}. (5)

The resulting Horn clauses are

∀a,α,κ.𝖺𝗋𝗍​_​𝗂​(a,α,κ)∧𝖼𝗅𝗂,𝗃​(κ)\displaystyle\forall a,\alpha,\kappa.\;{\sf art\_i}(a,\alpha,\kappa)\;\land\;{\sf cl_{i,j}}(\kappa)
→𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗁𝗂𝖻𝗂𝗍𝖾𝖽⁡(a,α,κ)∧𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗅𝗍𝗒⁡(a,α,κ)=pi,j.\displaystyle\rightarrow\;{\sf prohibited}(a,\alpha,\kappa)\;\land\;{\sf penalty}(a,\alpha,\kappa)=p_{i,j}. (6)

Formal Knowledge Base (KB). Each article in the criminal code is compiled into the above form, disambiguating cross-references (e.g., “Article 347(1)-(3)”) and parameterizing drug quantities, monetary thresholds, etc. This yields a static, searchable KB that the downstream LLMs and the solver query via an API layer.

Stage 2: Legal LLM Agents

Figure 1 (left half) depicts a symmetrical architecture that mirrors the real courtroom. Each statute is represented by a logical rule derived from Chinese Criminal Law, consisting of necessary conditions that must be satisfied for applicability. The Z3 solver evaluates these logical constraints against the extracted facts. If all conditions are met, the statute remains in the final set for sentencing; otherwise, it is filtered out and feedback to the prosecutor and attorney. The pipeline unfolds in the following micro-steps:

(a) Dual Fact–&–Statute Extractors.

The Prosecutor LLM and Attorney LLM receive the same free-text case narrative but are prompted with adversarial instructions (“maximise conviction” vs. “maximise acquittal”). Each produces:

  • •

    Fact tuples ℱ​⟨s,p,o,w⟩\mathcal{F}\langle s,p,o,w\rangle where w∈[0,1]w\in[0,1] encodes evidential confidence; and

  • •

    Candidate statute ranks S=[(i​d1,π1),…]S=[(id_{1},\pi_{1}),\dots] whose prior probabilities πi\pi_{i} stem from retrieval over the formal KB using dense embeddings.

The dual-extractor design prevents a single model from blending prosecution and defense biases, yet ensures both outputs conform to a unified JSON schema.

(b) Autoformalizer LLM.

A role-neutral LLM transforms ⟨ℱ,S⟩\langle\mathcal{F},S\rangle into well-typed Z3 assertions, interacting bidirectionally with 𝒦\mathcal{K} (grey double arrow). Concretely, it (i) ground-instantiates drug quantities, money thresholds, and temporal indices; (ii) resolves cross-referenced paragraphs (e.g., “Art. 347(1)&(3)”); and (iii) adds provenance tags so each axiom is traceable to its authoring agent.

(c) Iterative self-critique loop.

If Z3 reports unsat/undef, the solver returns a minimal unsat core, representing the smallest subset of formula that causes logical inconsistencies (Liffiton and Sakallah 2008). The Auto-Formalizer maps that core back to its textual origin (dashed arrow in the figure) and instructs the appropriate extractor to revise or drop only the offending clauses. We allow up to three such cycles, after which human jurists can step in.

(d) Formal Legal Reasoning.

Let Φ\Phi be the conjunction of formalized facts ℱ\mathcal{F} (grounds), instantiated statutes 𝒮\mathcal{S} (rules), and meta-constraints ℳ\mathcal{M} that encode hierarchical priority, temporal effect, and conflict-of-laws relationships.

  • •

    Consistency check: sat​(Φ)\textsf{sat}(\Phi) confirms that the party’s proposed rule set is not self-contradictory. An unsat core pinpoints the minimal conflicting statutes. For each type of cases, we have constructed a specific algorithm as in Table 2 to derive sentencing clauses.

  • •

    Verdict derivation: Assuming sat, we pose the query ∃p.𝗀𝗎𝗂𝗅𝗍𝗒⁡(p)\exists p.\,{\sf guilty}(p) and extract the model if proven. Sentencing severity is computed via an optimisation objective min⁡_​p​𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗅𝗍𝗒​(p)\min\_p~{\sf penalty}(p) subject to sentencing guidelines.

(e) Judge LLM.

Once Z3 returns a sat model, its proof object and the surviving statutes are passed to the Judge-LLM (red block), which then drafts (i) a declarative verdict (guilty / not guilty), (ii) a quantified sentence obtained via the optimisation query min⁡𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗅𝗍𝗒⁡(p)\min\,{\sf penalty}(p), and (iii) a narrative justification that references solver-derived facts, the relevant Code articles, and each party’s key arguments.

The design brings the following practical advantages: (a) role isolation improves faithfulness, (b) KB-grounded auto-formalization curbs hallucination, (c) the critique loop mimics adversarial litigation, (d) the formal reasoning enhance the model explainability, and (e) the Judge-LLM converts symbolic proofs into prose that stakeholders can audit. Together these steps operationalize interpretable, formally and verifiable legal reasoning at scale.

4 Experiments

We design a comprehensive evaluation to assess the effectiveness, robustness, and interpretability of our formal legal reasoning framework. Specifically, we investigate the following research questions:

  • •

    RQ1: How does our method perform compared to state-of-the-art baselines?

  • •

    RQ2: What is the contribution of different components of our method to final sentencing accuracy?

  • •

    RQ3: Does our method provide better robustness than baselines?

Datasets

We use two datasets in our experiments:

  • •

    LeCaRDv2 Subset Dataset: We construct a benchmark dataset based on LeCaRDv2 (Li et al. 2023a), a large-scale Chinese legal case retrieval dataset. For our experiments, we extract a subset of 11,200 cases within the criminal law. Each sample includes the full factual description of a criminal case, the corresponding applicable general and specific statutes, and the final judicial judgment.

  • •

    Synthetic Perturbation Dataset: To assess model robustness against factual variations, we construct a synthetic dataset by injecting legally meaningful modifications into base case descriptions. The perturbation generation process is guided by a rule set 𝒫\mathcal{P} derived from statutory triggers, where each rule pip_{i} specifies:

    • –

      Target statute: The legal provision lil_{i} expected to become applicable once the perturbation is applied.

    • –

      Perturbation text: A factual insertion describing circumstances that legally trigger lil_{i}.

    We create both single and combinatorial perturbations to simulate realistic factual changes, ensuring that each generated sample explicitly records: (i) the modified case text, (ii) updated statute sets G′G^{\prime}, (iii) the difference set Δ​G=G′∖G\Delta G=G^{\prime}\setminus G, and (iv) the applied perturbation types.

Table 3 shows the dataset statistics, including case counts, average lengths, and the average number of statutes.

Baselines.

We select a set of representative models to serve as baselines in our experiments.

  • •

    GPT‑4o: It is widely used for complex text analysis tasks, including legal domain applications, with strong reasoning and language understanding capabilities,

  • •

    GPT o4‑mini: It is optimized for structured logical inference and step-by-step reasoning, designed to provide efficient reasoning performance on challenging tasks.

  • •

    DeepSeek V3: A large model developed for enhanced logical reasoning, long-context handling, and robust inference in complex scenarios, with demonstrated effectiveness on reasoning benchmarks.

  • •

    Claude 4 Sonnet: An improved version of the Claude series with enhanced reasoning ability, better text organization, and reliable general-purpose performance.

  • •

    DISC‑LawLLM (Yue et al. 2023): A Chinese legal-domain large language model fine-tuned with hierarchical instruction design and retrieval-augmented corpus.

  • •

    LexiLaw (Li et al. 2024): A retrieval-augmented-generation(RAG) Chinese legal model that integrates a fine-tuned legal language model with external legal knowledge bases.

  • •

    GPT+RAG: A variant of GPT-4o augmented with an external retrieval module that supplies real statutory articles as contextual evidence during inference with our defined formal knowledge base.

Experiment Settings.

To be comparable to the baseline methods and reduce cost, we adopt GPT 4o in Stage 1 and o4-mini in Stage 2 and 3 of our approach (L4M), though this setup can be easily changed for future updates.

We design our experiments to evaluate two key aspects of model performance: (i) the ability to process real legal cases accurately, and (ii) the robustness of the model under input perturbations.

For the first aspect, we measure four indicators on LeCaRDv2 dataset through random sampling: Accuracy of General Provisions for predicting applicable general provisions, Accuracy of Specific Provisions for predicting applicable specific provisions, Average Sentencing Error (Months) for the mean absolute difference between predicted and actual sentence lengths, and Valid Sentencing Output Ratio for the proportion of cases producing a valid sentencing result.

For the second aspect, we assess robustness on Synthetic perturbation dataset using Change Accuracy, defined as the proportion of cases where the model correctly predicts changes in applicable legal provisions before and after a designed perturbation. Further details of the experimental setup and implementation can be found in Appendix.

4.1 RQ1: Accuracy Evaluation

We evaluate all models on identifying applicable general and specific provisions and to predict sentencing outcomes with minimal error. The task is framed as multi–label prediction, and we use Precision, Recall, and F1-score metrics for provision prediction. We also define Average Sentencing Error (Months) and Valid Ratio metrics as follows:

  1. (i)

    Average Sentencing Error (Months). Let lil_{i} be the ground-truth prison term (in months) for case ii and l^i\hat{l}_{i} the model prediction. We measure ASE=1N​∑i=1N|l^i−li|.\operatorname{ASE}=\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|\,\hat{l}_{i}-l_{i}\,|. ASE is the mean absolute error; lower is better.

  2. (ii)

    Valid Ratio (%). A prediction is deemed valid iff (a) it passes the SMT consistency check—i.e. the joint set of facts, predicted statutes, and sentence length is sat—and (b) l^i\hat{l}_{i} lies within the statutory range prescribed by each article in 𝒮^\hat{\mathcal{S}}.

Tables 4 and 5 show the results for general and specific provision prediction. Across both tasks, our L4M model clearly outperforms all baselines: on general-provision prediction it nearly doubles the next-best precision (0.31 vs 0.17) and boosts F1 from 0.24 to 0.35 while maintaining solid recall (0.40), and on specific-provision prediction it also delivers the top precision (0.78) and F1 (0.75). Vanilla LLMs (GPT-4o, DeepSeek v3, Claude 4 Sonnet) recall a fair share of relevant articles but pay for it in precision—e.g. DeepSeek v3 attains 0.45 recall yet only 0.10 precision. The results show that scaling model size or adding retrieval does little to restrain over-prediction. Explicit logical verification curbs hallucinations and prevents harmless but legally irrelevant statutes from polluting the result set.

Table 6 contrasts each model’s mean absolute sentencing error (in months) when the correct statutes are explicitly supplied (“with”) versus when the model must rely on its own statute selection (“without”).

First, statute grounding matters. General-purpose LLMs such as GPT-4o, GPT-o4-mini and DeepSeek-v3 show sizeable drops in error once the relevant provisions are fed in, confirming that much of their residual inaccuracy stems from misidentifying the governing articles. Conversely, domain-tuned systems (DISC-LawLLM, LexiLaw) actually degrade when statutes are injected, suggesting internal heuristics clash with the external signals.

Second, legal validity varies widely. DeepSeek-v3 achieves 14.9-month error, yet only 64% of its sentences with validity; GPT-o4-mini attains a high 0.94 validity but still errs by 26 months.

Finally, our L4M pipeline dominates on both fronts. With golden statutes it delivers the lowest error and the highest Valid Ratio (94.1 %), outperforming the next-best competitor by 4.1 months in accuracy and 3 percentage points in validity. The solver-anchored architecture therefore not only converts better statute recall into more precise sentences, but also acts as a safety net that filters out statutorily impermissible outcomes.

4.2 RQ2: Ablation Study

To assess the contribution of each component in our Legal LLM Agent framework (Figure 1), we conduct an ablation study comparing different model variants with our full pipeline. Table 7 reports three key metrics. G-F1 denotes the F1 score on general-provisions prediction, S-F1 is the F1 score on specific-provisions prediction, and SE (M) measures the sentencing error in months.

The performance of removing the attorney module drops G-F1 from 0.3459 to 0.3000 and raising the sentencing error to 20.00 months, showing that dual independent agents (prosecutor and attorney) provide complementary perspectives that enhance accuracy and robustness. Disabling all Z3-based reasoning produces the poorest G-F1 (0.1500) and the highest sentencing error (25.30 months), underscoring the critical role of formal logic in filtering incorrect statutes and ensuring reliable sentencing. In contrast, the full L4Msystem achieves the highest scores on both general and specific statute prediction and the lowest sentencing error, confirming its superior accuracy in legal decision-making.

4.3 RQ3: Robustness Evaluation

To evaluate the robustness of different models, we design controlled perturbations in case descriptions and assess their impact on predicted statutes. This experiment focuses on general provisions because they are more sensitive to fine-grained changes in factual circumstances (e.g., age of the offender, presence of surrender), while specific provisions are primarily determined by the main offense.

We define Change Accuracy as:

Change Accuracy=|{s∣s∈Spred∧s∈Strue}||Strue|\text{Change Accuracy}=\frac{\big|\{\,s\mid s\in S_{\text{pred}}\ \wedge\ s\in S_{\text{true}}\,\}\big|}{\big|\ S_{\text{true}}\ \big|}

where StrueS_{\text{true}} is the set of statutes whose applicability is altered by the designed perturbation, and SpredS_{\text{pred}} is the set of statutes predicted by the model after perturbation. The denominator considers only statutes affected by the change, excluding unrelated original provisions.

Results are reported in Table 8.

Our method (L4M) achieves a change accuracy of 56.25%, ranking first among all evaluated models. Most domain-specific baselines (DISC-LawLLM, LexiLaw) exhibit low or zero robustness, indicating limited adaptability to factual variations. The results highlight that our framework’s combination of agent-enhanced reasoning and formal logic validation provides better resilience to perturbations. Nonetheless, the robustness performance still depends on the accuracy of factual extraction from the underlying LLM, so errors in early-stage fact parsing can propagate and affect final statute prediction changes.

5 Discussion

Our results highlight the advantages of integrating formal logic with LLMs in legal AI. By decomposing the reasoning process into interpretable components, we offer a transparent legal pipeline that mirrors how human judges and lawyers reason through statutes.

Limitations:

Despite its promising results, our framework still faces three main challenges. First, its formalization quality is constrained by the accuracy of LLM outputs, so errors in identifying actors or conditions can propagate throughout the reasoning pipeline. Second, our current evaluation is limited to statutory rules, leaving the extension to case law, open-textured norms, and evolving jurisprudence as future work. Third, the system assumes deterministic rule parsing, which prevents it from fully capturing legal provisions that deliberately incorporate normative ambiguity.

Future Work:

Future research can extend our framework in several important directions. We envision building interactive legal agents capable of engaging in dialogue to clarify ambiguous case inputs, elicit missing information, or explain their outputs to human users. Besides, we plan to incorporate case-based reasoning and analogical inference to support legal systems where judicial precedents play a central role—enabling our framework to address common law reasoning and dynamically evolving jurisprudence.

6 Related Work

Recent progress in legal AI has led to the development of specialized LLM systems for the law.

Domain-specific Legal LLMs.

General-purpose LLMs often mishandle legal terminology and citation style. ChatLaw couples a knowledge-graph-enhanced mixture-of-experts backbone with a multi-agent pipeline that mirrors law-firm SOPs, outperforming GPT-4 on LawBench and national bar exams (Cui et al. 2023). Lawyer GPT shows that lightweight domain pre-training plus retrieval boosts statute-matching and consultation accuracy while remaining compute-efficient (Yao et al. 2024). Gao et al. (Gao et al. 2024) further show that careful construction of high-quality synthetic query–candidate pairs can markedly improve legal-case retrieval. Our work inherits this line of research but goes further by compiling the extracted norms into executable formal specifications.

Multi-agent Judicial Simulation.

Treating legal reasoning as collaboration among specialized agents has gained traction. Agents on the Bench simulates a collegial bench to improve judgment quality through deliberative voting (Jiang and Yang 2024), whereas AgentCourt evolves adversarial lawyer agents via long-horizon self-play, yielding measurable skill gains (Chen et al. 2024). These systems, however, lack guarantees on logical soundness. We retain the agent metaphor but ground each deliberation step in SMT-verified logic.

Neural–Symbolic Methods.

Hybrid approaches that blend neural representation learning with symbolic logic provide both adaptability and rigor. Early work such as Logic Tensor Networks (Badreddine et al. 2022) embeds many-valued fuzzy logic into differentiable architectures, while DeepProbLog (Manhaeve et al. 2018) integrates probabilistic logic programming with neural predicates. More recent studies add large-scale LLM components: NS-LCR learns explicit law- and case-level rules for explainable case retrieval (Sun et al. 2024); Logic-LM introduces structured prompting plus theorem-prover feedback to enforce logical soundness (Sadowski and Chudziak 2025); and Kant et al. combine neuro-symbolic reasoning with contract analysis to improve coverage decisions (Kant et al. 2025). These results show that logic grounding enhances transparency and robustness, which we pursue by marrying an agent-driven statute predictor with a symbolic criminal-law reasoner.

Governance and Liability.

Growing autonomy raises accountability questions. Gabison and Xian analyze principal–agent liability risks for LLM-based systems and highlight the need for technical audit trails (Gabison and Xian 2025). By outputting verifiable proofs and formal reasoning including facts and statues, our pipeline aligns with governance frameworks and facilitates post-hoc audits.

7 Conclusion

We present a new paradigm for legal AI that bridges the gap between natural language and formal legal reasoning. By extracting structured representations of legal norms, our system achieves interpretable, executable, and normatively faithful legal inference. Our experiments show that integrating formal logic improves both reasoning accuracy and transparency, making our system more aligned with the demands of real-world legal applications. As legal technology continues to evolve, combining language models with formal logic is not merely a technical convenience, but a necessary step toward building socially aligned AI systems.
